facts.text: Florence Nightingale was born in 1820 and is often remembered as the Lady with the Lamp because she made night rounds of the wards carrying a lamp.
In November 1854, during the Crimean War, Nightingale arrived at the British army's Barrack Hospital at Scutari, near Constantinople, leading a group of 38 nurses.
The Scutari hospital was crowded and dirty; its drains did not work properly and its water supply was contaminated.
During Nightingale's first winter at Scutari, 4,077 soldiers died, and about ten times as many died from diseases such as typhus, cholera and dysentery as from battle wounds.
Army deaths reached a peak in January 1855.
A government Sanitary Commission arrived in March 1855; it flushed the sewers, unblocked drains, improved ventilation and removed rubbish, and deaths from disease fell afterward.
After the war Nightingale worked with the government statistician William Farr to analyze army death records.
Nightingale used diagrams because the generals, officials and members of Parliament she wanted to persuade rarely read tables of statistics.
Her best-known diagram appeared in an 1858 report on the health of the British Army; each of its twelve wedges stands for one month.
In the diagram, blue wedges show deaths from preventable diseases, red wedges show deaths from wounds, and black wedges show deaths from other causes.
The diagram has two circles: one covers April 1854 to March 1855, before the sanitary improvements, and the other covers April 1855 to March 1856, after them.
In the circle for the later year, the blue wedges are much smaller than in the circle for the earlier year.
The diagrams were first given to Queen Victoria in a confidential report and later reissued for the general public.
Soon after the diagrams appeared, Parliament debated overcrowded army barracks and moved to reform sanitary conditions in the army, and military hospitals were improved.

Working with William Farr, Nightingale found that nearly seven times as many British soldiers died of disease as in combat during the war; deaths in the hospitals fell sharply once they were cleaned up.
In 1858 Nightingale became the first woman elected a member of the Royal Statistical Society.
